problem: What someone meant when they asked for a capability lives in their head, a chat or a task, and the code that answers it carries none of that meaning. Months later nobody, human or AI, can tell what a module was for, which use cases it must serve, or what "better" would mean for it.
who_has_it: The person who set the direction (Joshua, a Director), the developers and AI agents who change the code later, and anyone deciding whether a part is still needed.
why_it_matters: Code drifts from its purpose, work is redone, and the only way to judge a change is to read the implementation, which does not scale with AI writing most of the code.
why_hard: Words only approximate intent, intent changes over time, and many agents with no memory between sessions change the code faster than any document is kept current.
existing_attempts: Product requirement documents, architecture decision records, issue trackers, CLAUDE.md files and playbooks, code comments. They hold intent as prose that nothing checks against the code.

problem: Most parts of a system can be done several ways (a model tier, a router, a retrieval method), and the one in use was chosen by whoever wrote it, not by evidence. When a better alternative appears, nothing shows that it is better or makes it the default.
who_has_it: Maintainers and AI agents choosing or changing an implementation; Joshua, who wants the best implementation used automatically.
why_it_matters: Quality and cost depend on these choices. Real examples found once measured: a model priced at the wrong rate, a router kept although a cheaper one scored as well.
why_hard: Model output is noisy, costs swing with caching, good test cases are expensive to write, live runs cost money, and "best" differs per use case.
existing_attempts: Ad hoc evaluation scripts, public benchmarks, eval tools (promptfoo, OpenAI Evals, LangSmith), A/B testing platforms, experiment trackers. They measure, but do not tie the result to which implementation runs.

problem: A number recorded on uncommitted code, on a different case set, typed by hand, or copied into prose that is never updated looks like evidence but proves nothing. Two numbers from different conditions get compared as if they were alike.
who_has_it: Anyone deciding from a result: reviewers, Joshua, the selection itself.
why_it_matters: A wrong number leads to the wrong default, and once people notice untrustworthy numbers they stop reading metrics and go back to reading code.
why_hard: Provenance needs discipline every single time, several agents edit the same working copy at once, and noise makes small differences look real.
existing_attempts: Experiment trackers (MLflow, Weights and Biases), CI artifacts, lab notebooks, statistical significance tests.

problem: Switching a provider, runner or backend means finding and editing the call sites, often an `if` chain, and an embedding system cannot switch without forking.
who_has_it: Developers, operators configuring a deployment, and systems that embed a library built on this structure.
why_it_matters: Measuring an alternative is pointless if adopting it is risky and slow, so the measured winner never ships.
why_hard: Implementations need different configuration and optional dependencies, and a typo in a name must fail loudly rather than fall back silently.
existing_attempts: Dependency-injection containers, plugin entry points, feature-flag services, factory functions.

problem: Files no one can attribute to a purpose stay because deleting feels risky, and modules grow until no one reads them whole (one adapter file reached thousands of lines).
who_has_it: Maintainers, and AI agents whose context fills with code that does not matter to the task.
why_it_matters: Every unowned line costs reading, testing and risk, and hides the parts that matter.
why_hard: AI writes code faster than anyone prunes it, and without a record of purpose there is no basis to delete.
existing_attempts: Dead-code finders (vulture), code owners files, size linters, periodic clean-up passes.

problem: Rules written in prose (where files go, which way imports point, what must be documented) are followed by whoever read them and broken by the next agent, and generated documents drift from what they describe.
who_has_it: Maintainers and every agent working in the repository.
why_it_matters: The structure only gives its benefits while it holds; a rule broken once is copied.
why_hard: Agents start without memory, rules multiply, and a check that is slow or noisy gets skipped.
existing_attempts: Linters, pre-commit hooks, architecture tests (import-linter, ArchUnit), code review.

problem: A person who wants to steer quality has to read implementations, because ideals, metrics and current results are not gathered anywhere they can read and correct.
who_has_it: Joshua and the people who direct the work, who should be able to steer by reviewing metrics without having to read implementations.
why_it_matters: Review either does not happen or consumes the time it was meant to save, and human judgment never reaches the definition of "best".
why_hard: Results live across folders and repositories, a metric is only worth reviewing if it measures its ideal, and edits made in a review must flow back to the source.
existing_attempts: Dashboards, shared spreadsheets, pull-request review, status reports.

problem: Evaluations built beside production code test copies, stubs or scripts of their own, so their results describe something that does not run.
who_has_it: Joshua (who named this), maintainers deciding from results.
why_it_matters: A detached evaluation gives false confidence and decays as the real code changes.
why_hard: Driving real code needs realistic inputs, fakes for external services, and isolation from real data and spend.
existing_attempts: Integration tests, shadow traffic, canary releases, end-to-end tests against staging.

problem: A system builds on a library's solutions with its own stores and prompts, but cannot see which library solution each of its parts serves, whether its parts meet the library's own cases, or how far its pinned version lags.
who_has_it: Developers of any system built on a library that uses this structure.
why_it_matters: The embedding is where users meet the library, so an unsound integration undoes the library's quality.
why_hard: Two repositories, one public and one private, change at different rates under different rules.
existing_attempts: Version pins, changelogs, contract tests, integration test suites.

problem: The intent template is being refined in the skill, and every registry and checker that copied its fields falls out of date.
who_has_it: Joshua as the template's author, and every AI filling records.
why_it_matters: Records then follow an old idea of intent, and the author's refinements never reach the work.
why_hard: The template is prose written for people, and changing a field means changing every record that uses it.
existing_attempts: Copy and paste, schema documents, form builders.

problem: There is no worked, checked example of evolvable structure in code, so each team that wants it designs its own from prose.
who_has_it: Other developers and teams, open-source users of this library, AI agents asked to apply ESOI elsewhere.
why_it_matters: The approach only produces progress at scale if it is easy to copy.
why_hard: A standard has to be general enough for other repositories and concrete enough to follow without its author.
existing_attempts: Articles, framework conventions, project templates (cookiecutter).

problem: Every rule, record and check adds work to each change, and past a point contributors spend more time satisfying the structure than improving the code.
who_has_it: Contributors making small changes, and Joshua weighing the structure's value.
why_it_matters: Overbuilt structure gets bypassed, faked or abandoned, which loses its benefits entirely.
why_hard: The value of structure shows up later and spread out, while its cost is felt now on each change.
existing_attempts: Lightweight conventions, opt-in tooling, waivers.

problem: Results are stale when a choice depends on them, or paid runs happen with no decision behind them, so people either decide on numbers that no longer describe the code or stop running the metrics at all.
who_has_it: Maintainers and AI agents who choose between alternatives, and whoever pays for a run.
why_it_matters: A choice made on a stale number picks the wrong default, and money spent on a run nobody needed is gone. Either failure teaches people to distrust the metrics.
why_hard: Cheap and expensive metrics need different rhythms, the code changes faster than anyone re-records, noisy results tempt people to rerun until they like the answer, and a model or price can change under a result that was once true.
existing_attempts: Running everything in continuous integration, running nothing until a release, ad hoc scripts, and asking whoever remembers.

problem: A person who wants to use the author's skill cannot get it in a form that is both complete and safe to publish. The skill lives in a private folder next to material that is not public, so it cannot simply be shared; a copy made by hand starts to drift on the first edit; and a leaked name, path or internal process cannot be taken back once published.
who_has_it: Anyone outside the author's organization who wants to give their own agent the skill, and the author, who wants to publish it without maintaining two versions.
why_it_matters: Without a complete, current copy the skill is not used, or a stale partial one is used and teaches something the author no longer says. A leak costs trust and is permanent in a public history.
why_hard: The private folder mixes public and private material in the same files, the skill is refined often, an agent reads the files as plain text so any private fragment is read as instruction, and installing must work for people with no repository, no Python and no context.
existing_attempts: Copying files by hand, publishing the whole private folder, and skill registries or plugin marketplaces that distribute a folder but do not decide what may be in it.

problem: An AI agent asked to do work applies the principles inconsistently, and nothing shows how often. It builds a framework for a one-off fix, treats a task as a problem, merges use cases whose best differs into one function, drops the qualifier from a rule it restates, or pastes a fifth copy, and the instructions meant to prevent this (a skill, a system prompt) are edited with no measure showing whether the behaviour got better or worse.
who_has_it: People who direct AI agents and want their principles applied (Joshua, a team lead), the authors of the skills and prompts that carry those principles, and the agents themselves, which start each session without memory of earlier corrections.
why_it_matters: AI writes most of the work, so reading every reply or implementation does not scale, and a principle that is not applied is not a principle. Structure that people can steer only by reading output brings back the problem that structure exists to remove.
why_hard: Replies are open-ended; acting by a principle often means holding back from adding structure or keeping a qualifier; the same words can be used while doing the opposite; models vary between runs and versions; and each live measurement costs money.
existing_attempts: Writing the principles into a skill or a system prompt, correcting the agent in conversation, reading samples of its output by hand, public language-model benchmarks and eval tools (promptfoo, OpenAI Evals, LangSmith). They test general ability or one prompt at a time, and do not tie a measure of adherence to which instructions are used.

problem: People who want to apply ESOI have the five record types and the principles but no order to follow. They do not know what to do first, write implementations before deciding what best means, trust a metric nobody checked, skip the perspectives that would find gaps, and stop after the first build instead of looping back.
who_has_it: Anyone applying ESOI to a project, product, course, process or code for the first time, the AI agents asked to apply it, and people who apply it often but skip steps under time pressure.
why_it_matters: The records only optimize an intent when they are made in an order that decides best before building and keeps measuring after; without an order, ESOI is applied partially and the parts that address the biggest risks are the ones skipped.
why_hard: The work is a network, not a line, so any order is a simplification; small tasks and large projects need very different depth; and the order has to change as ESOI itself changes.
existing_attempts: The 2020 Project Documentation board checklist (an order, but without metric checks, interfaces, the split test, perspectives or retirement); the one-hour guide in this repository (a short pass, no full order); general project-management and design-thinking processes, which do not compare implementations by metric.

problem: Where ESOI is already applied, how those projects relate and where to look in each is rediscovered in every session.
who_has_it: People and AI agents who apply ESOI to more than one project on the same machine or board.
why_it_matters: Time goes to finding structure that already exists, and a new session may build again what a neighbouring project already solved.
why_hard: Projects live in different places, use different layouts and change, so any list written once into the guidance goes stale and names projects the reader does not work on.
existing_attempts: Routing rows written into a skill's index for known projects, a project's own CLAUDE.md, and memory of past sessions.

problem: A model that grades whether a reply acts by the principles can disagree with the people whose intent the principles express, can favour its own phrasing when it wrote the reply, and can pass a reply that uses the right words while doing the opposite. Nothing shows by how much, so a score built on its verdicts looks like evidence but may measure the judge.
who_has_it: Joshua and others who review the behaviour metric to steer, and the maintainers who choose instructions by that metric.
why_it_matters: A miscalibrated judge makes the behaviour metric steer toward whatever the judge likes. A reviewer who finds its verdicts wrong stops trusting the metric and goes back to reading output, which is the problem of untrusted measurements again.
why_hard: The people whose verdicts would calibrate it are few and their time is the scarcest input; the labelled replies are written by the same author as the checks, so agreement can be circular; and a judge changes whenever the model behind it does.
existing_attempts: Pattern checks alone, which agree with their author by construction; using the strongest available model as judge without measuring it; agreement statistics on small samples; hand review of every verdict.

problem: The records repeat what the code already says: which alternatives of a solution exist, the file each lives in, and an interface's signature. Each repeated fact is kept in step by hand, or by a check that only reports the drift, so adding an alternative means editing the code and several records, and the two drift apart.
who_has_it: Developers and AI agents who add or change an alternative, and the reviewers who trust the records to describe the code.
why_it_matters: A second copy held in step by a check is upkeep, not structure. It is skipped under deadline, and a record that disagrees with the code is worse than none.
why_hard: Most of a record is intent only a person can write (the problem, the ideal, the metric), so the records cannot simply be generated from the code. Only what the code already states may be derived, and a person's text must never be overwritten.
existing_attempts: Documentation generators and schema tools derive pages from code; plugin registries and dependency-injection decorators declare alternatives in code; none keep intent records in step with them.

problem: A rival that clearly beats the selected implementation on the solution's own metric stays unadopted until someone notices and edits the selection, the metric's command and the record of why, by hand.
who_has_it: Maintainers and AI agents, and the people who steer by metrics and want the best implementation used.
why_it_matters: Measuring an alternative is pointless if adopting the winner is a chore, and the evidence for a switch is scattered or lost.
why_hard: A switch must not rest on a result without provenance, on different cases, or on code that has since changed. A person may want to approve some switches. A selection table that holds its own default would then disagree with the records.
existing_attempts: Model registries and deployment gates promote a model past a metric threshold; ranking boards show who is ahead without switching anything.

problem: An intent's folder of CSV files states it completely, but what the intent is for cannot be seen without opening several files and following ids between them.
who_has_it: Newcomers, reviewers and AI agents who open an intent's folder.
why_it_matters: Records nobody can read at a glance are not reviewed, and hand-written summaries beside them repeat the records and drift from them.
why_hard: A readable page must never disagree with the records, so it cannot be hand-kept, and a person's own prose about the network is theirs and has to stay.
existing_attempts: A README per folder written by hand; spreadsheets for review; generated indexes of components.

problem: An arm that meters a deterministic stand-in for a model counts the calls a real model would make but spends nothing. It is recorded with an unknown model and cost, so the harness skips it as paid and the ranking rates a free baseline cheaper than a cost that is merely unknown, reporting a loss that is not real.
who_has_it: Maintainers of a project whose evaluations run offline stand-ins beside paid model arms.
why_it_matters: A false loss sends a person to fix a selection that is right, and a skipped arm leaves its result stale.
why_hard: A missing price looks the same for a free stand-in and for a paid model whose price was never entered, so being free cannot be inferred from the cost alone; the arm has to declare itself.
existing_attempts: Listing the arm as paid in configuration, or recording a zero cost by hand.

problem: The default implementation of a solution is written in the selection table and again in the records, and only a check holds the two equal. Choosing a winner means editing both, and a mismatch fails the build.
who_has_it: Developers who embed the esoi package and keep a selection table, and whoever promotes a winner.
why_it_matters: Two copies of one decision are upkeep: the default that runs and the recorded one drift, and the recorded one is the one the metric decides.
why_hard: The table is read in other people's running code, which may not ship the records, so the default has to reach it some way other than a second hand-kept copy.
existing_attempts: Defaults repeated in configuration per environment; feature-flag services; a check that compares the copies.

problem: Making a part swappable takes a port class, a table entry with an import path for every alternative, a wrapper file to measure each one, and edits wherever the choice is made, so most parts are never made swappable.
who_has_it: Developers who want an alternative to be a name in a call, not a refactor.
why_it_matters: A part that cannot be swapped cannot be measured against a rival or tuned for a deployment, so the best implementation is never found.
why_hard: Alternatives need different configuration and optional dependencies, a typo has to fail loudly, the choice differs by call, test, deployment and environment, and the code may live in packages the project does not own.
existing_attempts: Dependency-injection containers, plugin entry points, strategy-pattern factories, and in the author's earlier work a decorator that declares a stage once and a call that swaps an implementation by its name.

problem: A rule is kept in code with no record of the mistake that justified it or of what it has caught since, so nobody can tell whether it still earns its place or why its limit has its value.
who_has_it: Maintainers deciding whether to keep, change or drop a rule.
why_it_matters: Rules multiply and each adds work to every change; a rule that catches nothing is pure cost, and one with an unexplained limit gets waived or copied.
why_hard: A rule is a function whose reason lives in its author's head, the ids carry no meaning, and what a rule catches is not logged.
existing_attempts: Comments in the rule code; the generated list of rules; review.

problem: A new use case or input arrives, and nobody (human or AI) can tell which of a project's problems, ideals, solutions, implementations and metrics apply without reading all of them. The specifications exist, but finding the relevant few is left to whoever happens to remember them.
who_has_it: An AI system or person applying a project's specifications to a new request, and the maintainers of a repository whose records have outgrown one reading.
why_it_matters: Applying the wrong specifications, or none, loses the intent behind a request; loading all of them costs tokens and attention and drowns the relevant ones. Reuse of ESOI depends on reaching the right record at the right moment.
why_hard: Words in a request rarely match a record's own words; records are linked, so a good hit's neighbours matter too; the cheap lexical step must narrow without discarding the right record, and semantic search and a model's final choice belong to a system on top, not to this library.
existing_attempts: Reading the folder's README; grep over the CSV files; a vector store with a model's final selection (the Quest AI runner's retrieval); the local ESOI index, which routes to projects, not to records.

problem: A metric scores a scripted judge, a mocked model or a canned answer instead of the real thing, so its number measures the plumbing around the thing and not the thing. A perfect scripted judge passes everything, and a decision built on the number is backed by nothing.
who_has_it: Anyone choosing between alternatives by a metric, and the people who review the metric instead of the implementations.
why_it_matters: Review by metric only works if the metric is real; a stand-in number looks like evidence and sends a person to adopt, or keep, the wrong implementation.
why_hard: A stand-in is the easy way to make a model-backed metric cheap, fast and repeatable, and a scripted run does test something real (the plumbing), so the number looks respectable.
existing_attempts: Declaring the arm SIMULATED so the harness does not rank it as paid; unit tests of the plumbing. Neither stops a stand-in from being a solution's only metric.
